Oil Painting is the technique of applying pigments mixed with linseed or other drying oils to canvas, wood panel, or other surfaces. Developed in early Renaissance Flanders and perfected across Europe, oil became the dominant medium of Western art for over five centuries. The medium's slow drying time allows for blending, layering, glazing, and revisions impossible with tempera or fresco. Its richness of color and luminosity lends itself to subtle modeling and psychological depth. From Jan van Eyck through the old masters to contemporary practice, oil painting remains synonymous with fine art itself, valued for its material permanence, expressive range, and capacity to render both precise detail and atmospheric effect.

Oil painting developed in Flanders in the early fifteenth century; Jan van Eyck is often credited as a pioneer, though the technique likely evolved gradually. It replaces tempera, the egg-based medium, as the dominant medium by the sixteenth century due to its superior handling, blending, and luminosity.

The medium is composed of pigment suspended in drying oil, typically linseed oil. The slow drying enables reworking, layering, and glazing—building up transparent layers of color over time. Oil allows for unprecedented color saturation, subtle transitions using the sfumato technique, and the modeling of light and shadow through chiaroscuro.

Technical mastery required understanding of underpainting, layering using the fat-over-lean principle, glazing, and the chemical properties of drying oils and pigments. Oil painting was the material medium of choice for the Renaissance, Baroque, Romantic, and much of Modernism, becoming synonymous with high art and fine craftsmanship.

Oil's environmental toxicity and long drying time have led to increasing use of acrylics and other synthetic media in contemporary practice, yet oil remains culturally prestigious. Artists continue to work in oil, drawn to its unique handling properties and the depth it allows.
